item.title: Anthropic lines up $26 billion from Nvidia, Google, others as IPO priced at $70 to $80
item.description:
The placement de-risks the deal at a fragile moment for AI stocks. Locking in $26 billion of demand before launch makes a weak debut less likely and could steady sentiment across AI names if pricing goes well. The supplier-as-investor structure may also feed concerns about circular financing in the AI sector, the same theme that has weighed on credit spreads and hyperscaler funding. For the wider market, the final price and implied valuation will set a benchmark for AI valuations after last week’s selloff. A deal priced at the top of the range would point to resilient appetite, while one at the bottom would suggest the reset has further to run.

----

Anthropic is going to market with its biggest suppliers as anchor buyers, a show of support that both steadies the deal and sharpens questions about who is funding the AI boom.

Summary:

  • Anthropic plans to sell about 867 million new shares at $70 to $80 each, raising up to about $69 billion, according to a filing seen by Reuters
  • Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC will invest a combined $26 billion through a private placement at the IPO price
  • The IPO and placement combined would raise roughly $87 billion to $95 billion; the IPO alone falls short of SpaceX’s roughly $75 billion record
  • The implied valuation was not disclosed
  • Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT” as soon as Thursday or Friday next week

Anthropic has lined up $26 billion from some of the biggest names in technology to buy shares alongside its initial public offering, setting terms for what could become the largest capital raise of any stock market debut.

The Claude maker plans to sell about 867 million new shares at $70 to $80 each, raising up to about $69 billion, according to a filing seen by Reuters. Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC will together invest a further $26 billion through a private placement at the IPO price.

Combined, the IPO and the placement would bring in roughly $87 billion to $95 billion. Even at the top of its range, the IPO alone falls short of the record of around $75 billion that SpaceX set in June, but the total including the placement would exceed it. Some early reports described the IPO as record-breaking, which holds only when the placement is included. The implied valuation has not been disclosed, because the total number of shares outstanding after the offering was not reported.

The list of anchor investors stands out. Every company named sells chips, memory or cloud capacity to AI developers, making them both suppliers to Anthropic and now shareholders. That ties the deal closely to the wider debate over how the AI build-out is being financed, and how much of it is funded by companies that also benefit from the spending.

The commitments come a week after a sharp selloff in AI stocks, when the Nasdaq Composite shed about $2.5 trillion in value following the US midterm elections. The Wall Street Journal had reported that some major investors were pushing Anthropic to accept a valuation below the roughly $1.5 trillion previously expected, and well below the $2 trillion floated months ago. Securing large committed buyers at the IPO price before launch reduces the risk of weak demand in a nervous market.

Anthropic is aiming for its shares to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT” as soon as Thursday or Friday next week, according to the Journal. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are advising on the deal. The final price, and the valuation it implies, will be the clearest test yet of public market appetite for AI after the recent rout.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australian consumer sentiment sinks to four-year low as rates and living costs bite
item.description:
Together with this morning’s NAB survey, the reading strengthens the case for an RBA pause in December and lowers the odds of a sixth hike. That leaves the Australian dollar with little support from rate expectations, at a time when it is already exposed to swings in AI-linked equities. Front-end Australian bond yields are the most sensitive to any shift toward pricing an earlier end to the tightening cycle. Above-target inflation and petrol prices near A$2.40 a litre keep the RBA from pivoting quickly. Lower oil prices would be the fastest route to relief for households.

-

Australian households are feeling as gloomy as they have only in genuine crises, and the RBA’s own rate hikes are a big part of why.

Summary:

  • The Westpac-Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment Index fell 2.7% to 78.2 in November, the lowest since late 2022
  • Readings this weak have otherwise only been seen during COVID, the global financial crisis and the recessions of the early 1980s and 1990s
  • Higher petrol prices, 4.3% inflation and a fifth RBA hike this year, to 4.85%, are driving the gloom; mortgage holders’ sentiment hit a record low
  • More than 70% of consumers expect mortgage rates to keep rising, and house price expectations turned negative
  • Westpac expects the RBA to pause in December and does not expect a hike in February

Australian consumer sentiment fell to a four-year low in November, as rising living costs and another interest rate hike pushed households deeper into pessimism, a Westpac and Melbourne Institute survey showed on Tuesday.

The Westpac-Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment Index dropped 2.7% to 78.2 from 80.4 in October, its weakest reading since late 2022. Westpac noted that, apart from that period, readings this low have only been seen in the economy’s darkest moments, including the onset of the COVID pandemic, the global financial crisis and the recessions of the early 1990s and 1980s.

Cost-of-living pressure remains the main driver. Over the past month petrol prices have pushed toward A$2.40 a litre and official inflation has reached 4.3%. The Reserve Bank of Australia has also raised the cash rate by another 25 basis points to 4.85%, an 18-year high. Westpac said any lift from the US midterm results had been swamped by inflation and rate worries. Sentiment among mortgage holders slumped to a record low on data back to 1994.

The November fall was led by a sharp deterioration in near-term expectations for the economy, which dropped to their weakest since August 2020. Households also turned negative on house prices for the first time since late 2022, and more than 70% of consumers expect mortgage rates to rise further over the coming year. Job-loss fears are edging higher, though Westpac described consumers as on edge rather than alarmed.

For the RBA, the survey adds to evidence that its five hikes this year are biting hard on rate-sensitive parts of the economy. Westpac expects the central bank to pause at its December 7-8 meeting to assess the impact of its tightening. It does not expect a hike in February either, though it cautioned that high inflation will continue to test the bank’s resolve.

The weak mood is a concern for retailers heading into Christmas. Even so, Westpac said gift-spending intentions have held up better than headline sentiment suggests, with mortgage holders the most likely to cut back.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: The view from China: CITIC sees Iran war risk ‘bounded’ as blockade outlasts US midterms
item.description:
CITIC’s “bounded” framing points oil toward a range rather than a trend. Limited escalation risk caps the upside for crude, while the absence of a negotiated exit keeps Iranian barrels off the market and Hormuz traffic restricted, which puts a floor under prices. That fits this week’s pattern of de-escalation headlines failing to drive a lasting sell-off. For traders, the main risks to the range are a surprise diplomatic breakthrough, which CITIC sees as unlikely, or an escalation that Congress and US public opinion fail to restrain.

---

From Beijing’s vantage point, the Iran war has settled into a stalemate that neither escalates nor ends, with the US blockade as its defining feature.

Summary:

  • CITIC Securities says Republican midterm losses do not necessarily change the course of the US-Iran conflict
  • It expects the Trump administration to maintain a high-pressure economic blockade, keeping war risk “bounded”
  • Escalation is restrained by Congress’s control of war funding, US public opposition to a long war, and Israel’s reliance on US backing
  • De-escalation is blocked because Iran’s demands are unacceptable to both US parties and Washington lacks an exit strategy
  • The view matches recent signals: Trump favours keeping the blockade, while Tehran demands it be lifted first

The view from China: Republican losses in the US midterm elections do not necessarily change the trajectory of the US-Iran conflict, according to CITIC Securities. The brokerage expects the Trump administration to keep up a high-pressure economic blockade on Tehran and the war to stay contained within clear limits.

The Chinese brokerage describes Middle East war risk as being in a bounded state. In its view, the risk of escalation is controllable, while a negotiated de-escalation remains blocked. It argues that Iran’s strategic aims leave no room for compromise with either of the main US parties.

CITIC sees several brakes on escalation. Congress holds leverage over war funding, and US public opposition to a prolonged conflict with Iran reduces the political payoff from widening it. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also has limited scope to expand operations without US backing.

At the same time, the brokerage sees little prospect of a negotiated exit. It says Iran’s strategic demands are unacceptable to Democrats and Republicans alike, and Washington lacks a feasible exit strategy. That leaves the conflict stuck between the two extremes.

The assessment matches the latest signals from both sides. US President Donald Trump said this week that renewed military action looks unlikely and that Gulf states prefer to keep the naval blockade in place. Meanwhile, Iran’s top security official told Washington to accept Tehran’s seven conditions, including an end to the blockade, before any talks.

For oil, a bounded conflict cuts both ways. A lower risk of escalation limits the scope for a renewed spike in prices. But a blockade with no exit keeps Iranian supply constrained and the Strait of Hormuz disrupted, leaving a floor under crude.

---

CITIC Securities is one of China’s largest securities firms and is widely described as its biggest brokerage. Founded in 1995, it offers investment banking, brokerage, research and asset management, and is listed in Shanghai and Hong Kong. It is part of the state-owned CITIC Group conglomerate and owns the regional broker CLSA, which runs much of its international business.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UK retail sales rise 1.5%, best since June, but fuel costs and Budget caution weigh
item.description:
The data give a mixed signal for UK rates and sterling. Headline spending is firmer, but much of the gain reflects higher fuel prices, so it shows energy costs rather than stronger real demand. That supports the view that the oil shock is acting as a tax on households, which tends to weigh on discretionary spending and confidence over time. Flat non-food sales and the weakest confidence since April argue against reading the numbers as a pickup in underlying consumer momentum. Any easing in oil prices from Middle East de-escalation would offer households relief at the pump, while the Budget remains a near-term source of caution for spending and for the pound.

-

Earlier:

  • Markets price three more BoE hikes, but analysts see a shallower path after move to 4%

-

Britons spent more in October, but mostly on fuel and food, and they feel gloomier about the economy than at any point since April.

Summary:

  • BRC total retail sales rose 1.5% year on year in October, from 1.3% in September and the strongest since June; like-for-like sales rose 1.1%
  • Food sales rose 3.2% while non-food sales were flat, with some shoppers waiting for Black Friday deals
  • Higher household costs and caution ahead of the Budget kept growth modest
  • Barclays card spending rose 2.3%, the biggest increase since July 2025, with essential spending up 3.1% on a 22.7% jump in fuel spending
  • Barclays’ consumer confidence gauge fell to its weakest since April

UK retail sales grew modestly in October, the British Retail Consortium said on Tuesday. Higher petrol prices, caution ahead of the Budget and shoppers holding off for Black Friday deals kept a lid on spending, even as a separate card-spending survey from Barclays showed the strongest growth in more than a year.

Total retail sales rose 1.5% from a year earlier, up from 1.3% in September and the strongest increase since June, according to the BRC. Like-for-like sales, which strip out changes in store space, rose 1.1% after 1.0% the previous month. Food sales climbed 3.2% while non-food sales were flat, a split that points to price-driven grocery spending rather than a broad pickup in discretionary demand. The BRC noted that sales of cupboard staples rose modestly after the government advised households to stock up for emergencies.

Commentary accompanying the survey described overall growth as modest, citing higher household costs, caution ahead of the Budget and consumers waiting for Black Friday discounts.

Barclays’ data, which covers card spending on a wider range of goods and services, painted a firmer picture. Consumer spending rose 2.3% year on year in October, up from 2.0% in September and the biggest increase since July 2025. Essential spending grew 3.1%, driven by a 22.7% jump in spending on fuel, while non-essential spending rose 1.9%. Entertainment had its strongest month since September 2024 as tickets for the Glastonbury music festival went on sale.

The fuel figure shows how higher energy costs are inflating headline spending. Much of the increase reflects households paying more at the pump rather than buying more, which squeezes budgets for other goods.

That strain shows up in sentiment. Barclays said consumer confidence in the UK economy was at its weakest since April, suggesting households remain wary despite the steadier spending figures. Non-food sales were flat, and Black Friday is likely to pull some purchases into late November. That leaves October’s numbers as a mixed read on UK consumer demand heading into the key holiday trading period. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia business conditions hit six-year low as forward orders slide: NAB
item.description:
The survey strengthens the case that the RBA’s five hikes this year are biting, and lowers the odds of a sixth. Elevated input costs and underlying inflation well above target still argue against any early pivot to easing. That leaves the cash rate on hold at 4.85%, a stance that offers the Australian dollar little support from rate expectations. Softer domestic data compound the pressure on the Aussie, which is already trading as a proxy for AI-linked equity sentiment. Australian bond yields at the front end are the most likely to respond if markets start pricing cuts further out.

--

Australian firms are being squeezed from both sides, with demand fading and costs still climbing, which is exactly the bind the RBA now faces.

Summary:

  • NAB’s business conditions index fell 1 point to -2 in October, the lowest since August 2020, as forward orders dropped sharply
  • Business confidence fell 1 point to -15, far below its long-run average of +5
  • Retail reported the weakest confidence, conditions and forward orders, and construction also softened
  • Purchase cost growth rose 0.1 percentage point to a quarterly 2.4%
  • NAB says cost pressures remain a risk to inflation while slowing growth threatens labour demand
  • The RBA has hiked five times this year to 4.85%, an 18-year high; underlying inflation was 3.6% in September

Australian business conditions fell to their weakest level in six years in October as forward orders dropped sharply, a National Australia Bank survey showed on Tuesday. The survey points to slowing domestic demand under the weight of higher borrowing costs and persistent cost pressures.

The survey’s business conditions index slipped 1 point to -2, the lowest reading since August 2020. Business confidence also fell 1 point, to -15, far below its long-run average of +5. NAB said conditions have been trending gradually lower in recent months, suggesting growth has slowed further in the second half of 2026 from an already softer first half.

Retail reported the weakest confidence, conditions and forward orders of any industry. Construction, which had held up well this year, also showed signs of softening.

Costs remain a sticking point. Purchase cost growth picked up 0.1 percentage point to a quarterly rate of 2.4%, keeping input price pressures elevated even as demand slows.

That combination sums up the Reserve Bank of Australia’s dilemma, according to NAB. The bank said cost pressures remain a serious risk to the inflation outlook, but growth is slowing and labour demand may soften in the months ahead. The RBA has raised rates five times this year, taking the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85%, in response to stubborn inflation. Underlying inflation was running at an annual 3.6% in September, well above the central bank’s 2% to 3% target band.

The survey adds to signs that the RBA’s tightening is biting. With forward orders falling and confidence deeply negative, the case for further hikes looks weaker, though elevated costs and above-target inflation make an early shift toward easing unlikely. For the Australian dollar, already under pressure from the slide in AI-linked stocks, softer domestic data add another reason for caution. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6655 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BoJ opinions back faster hikes, one sees neutral rate ‘considerably above 1%’
item.description:
The Summary should firm pricing for a December hike to 1.5% and support the yen against the US dollar. It could also lift short-dated Japanese government bond yields, since the debate is now about pace, not direction. The member putting neutral considerably above 1% matters for terminal-rate pricing: it suggests markets could push their end-point expectations higher than the roughly 2% some already pencil in for next year. The dovish checks, notably weak consumption reinforced by today’s 6.8% household spending slump, limit the case for a faster-than-quarterly pace for now. The view that the policy rate is already within the neutral range is the main counterweight. Higher oil prices, which members flagged as pushing up inflation, keep the energy link to BoJ policy live.

---

The BoJ’s argument is no longer about whether to keep hiking but how fast, and the hawks are making the louder case.

Summary:

  • The BoJ board judged underlying inflation to be generally consistent with its 2% target, shifting the debate to the pace of hikes
  • One member called for stepping up the pace to neutral, another urged reaching it soon but to “make haste slowly”, and a third backed getting there early
  • One member said the neutral rate is likely considerably above 1%; core CPI is projected to exceed 3% toward the end of the fiscal year
  • More cautious members cited the lagged effects of past hikes, and one warned the policy rate is already within the estimated neutral range
  • Members flagged weak consumption momentum and uncertainty over how long AI-related demand will last; they also backed faster ETF sales
  • The Summary supports expectations for a hike to 1.5% at the December 17-18 meeting

Bank of Japan policymakers broadly agreed at their October meeting that the next move is a further rate hike, according to the Summary of Opinions released on Tuesday. Several pushed to reach the neutral rate soon, and one argued that neutral is likely “considerably above 1 percent.”

The summary, an anonymous digest of views from the October 29 and 30 meeting, shows the board judged underlying inflation to be generally consistent with the 2% price target. With that point settled, the debate has moved from whether to hike to how quickly. One member described a “new phase” in which the bank needs to step up the pace of bringing rates to neutral, noting that the effects of past hikes have yet to materialise and financial conditions remain accommodative. Another said the bank should reach neutral soon but “make haste slowly,” checking financial conditions for a few months after each move. A third called for a regime shift to get rates to neutral at an early stage, giving the bank room to respond nimbly in either direction.

Inflation risks featured prominently. Members noted that core CPI is projected to exceed 3% toward the end of the fiscal year and that inflation has picked up with the rise in crude oil prices. They also said Japan’s inflation expectations are less firmly anchored than those in Europe or the US, leaving the economy more exposed to external shocks.

The more cautious voices were also on record. Some members favoured holding in October to examine risks and the cumulative effect of past hikes. One said underlying inflation can be anchored around 2% without hastily raising rates to neutral. Another warned that with the policy rate already within the estimated neutral range, a further hike could weigh on the economy.

Consumption was a recurring concern. One member said private consumption lacks momentum and is unlikely to lead the economy. Another said the bank should not be overly cautious about the next hike but should assess the underlying trend in spending. That point gained weight on Tuesday, when data showed September household spending fell 6.8% from a year earlier, far worse than expected.

Members also flagged uncertainty over how long AI-related demand will support Japan’s economy, and backed the decision to speed up the bank’s ETF sales. Government representatives said they expect the bank to cooperate closely with the government. Taken together, the summary supports market expectations for a hike to 1.5% at the December 17-18 meeting, with consumption and next year’s wage talks the main checks on the pace. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan household spending plunges 6.8%, 10th straight drop, as BoJ weighs December hike
item.description:
The miss adds a dovish counterweight just as traders look to the Summary of Opinions for confirmation of a December hike. That could temper the yen’s gains from rate expectations in the near term. A strong hawkish tone in the Summary would likely outweigh one weak, volatile data point, leaving December pricing broadly intact. If the Summary instead shows members giving more weight to soft demand, the data would reinforce a slower path and leave the yen more exposed. Japanese government bond yields at the short end are the cleanest gauge of how markets weigh the two.

---

Earlier:

  • Event calendar in Asia Tuesday, November 10, 2026: BoJ and China trade data

---

Japanese households are still keeping their wallets shut despite higher pay, giving the BoJ’s cautious members fresh ammunition just as the hawks push for December.

Summary:

  • Japan’s household spending fell 6.8% year on year in September, against a forecast 3.1% fall, and dropped 2.8% month on month versus an expected 0.3% rise
  • It was the 10th straight annual decline and far deeper than July’s 3.6% fall, the previous 30-month low
  • Real wages had risen for eight months through August, but higher pay is not yet showing up in spending
  • The BoJ held at 1.25% in October on an 8-1 vote, with one member backing a hike to 1.5%, and trimmed its fiscal 2027 growth forecast
  • The Summary of Opinions from that meeting is the next test; markets widely expect a December hike

Japanese household spending fell far more sharply than expected in September. The weak consumption signal comes just as the Bank of Japan publishes the Summary of Opinions from its October meeting and markets weigh the case for a December rate hike.

Spending fell 6.8% from a year earlier, internal affairs ministry data showed, against a median forecast for a 3.1% decline. On a seasonally adjusted monthly basis, spending dropped 2.8%, compared with expectations for a 0.3% rise. It was the tenth consecutive year-on-year decline and far deeper than July’s 3.6% drop, which had itself been the steepest in 30 months. August had shown a smaller 3.1% fall.

The weakness persists even though real wages had risen for eight straight months through August, suggesting higher pay is still being absorbed by elevated living costs rather than spent. The household survey is volatile and based on a relatively small sample, so economists tend to treat single readings with caution. Even so, the run of declines is now hard to dismiss.

The data feed directly into the debate inside the BoJ. The central bank held its policy rate at 1.25% on October 30 in an 8-1 vote, with board member Hajime Takata dissenting in favour of a hike to 1.5%. It said underlying inflation is now generally consistent with its 2% target and judged price risks to be skewed to the upside, while trimming its fiscal 2027 growth forecast to 0.7%. Governor Kazuo Ueda later softened the inflation message at his press conference.

The Summary of Opinions is an anonymous digest of board members’ views, released ahead of the full minutes. It will show how many policymakers see the conditions for the next hike as in place, and how much weight the more cautious members give to the economy. Soft consumption is the kind of evidence those members could cite, alongside the slightly weaker growth outlook.

For now, markets widely expect the BoJ to keep its roughly quarterly pace with a hike in December, after moves in June and September. The policy board’s focus remains on inflation and wages rather than any single spending print. But a sustained slide in household demand would make it harder for the bank to argue that higher wages are feeding through to a self-sustaining recovery. It could also leave the yen with less support from rate expectations. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US CPI preview: 43-day shutdown leaves no official annual rate as monthly pace seen easing
item.description:
With no official annual rate, the monthly core reading carries most of the weight. A 0.3% core print would revive hawkish Fed pricing for December, likely lifting Treasury yields and the dollar and adding pressure to tech stocks still fragile after last week’s selloff. A 0.2% or softer core reading would support the case for a pause and help extend Monday’s equity rebound. Estimated annual headline figures near 4% may still dominate early headlines, so there is a risk of a knee-jerk move that fades once traders focus on the monthly detail. Lower gasoline prices during October offer some relief on the energy side.

--

The monthly numbers should show prices rising more slowly than in September, but the shutdown gap means the annual inflation rate everyone quotes will be an estimate this time.

Summary:

  • The BLS releases October CPI at 13:30 GMT (08:30 US Eastern time); consensus sees headline up about 0.3% m/m and core about 0.2%, after 0.6% and 0.3% in September
  • Last year’s 43-day shutdown means there is no October 2025 index, so the BLS will not publish 12-month changes for headline or core
  • FactSet’s estimates imply headline inflation of about 4% y/y (from 3.7%) and core of about 2.8% (from 2.6%), but these are imputed, not official
  • Analysts see risks to core tilted higher: shipping costs, reinstated tariffs, airfares and lodging, partly offset by softer owners’ equivalent rent
  • It is the final CPI before the Fed’s December meeting; the Fed held in October, and an in-line print would not rule out further tightening

US consumer prices are expected to have risen at a slower monthly pace in October after a gasoline-driven jump in September. But Tuesday’s report will arrive with a notable gap: there will be no official annual inflation rate for either the headline or the core index.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the October CPI at 13:30 GMT (08:30 US Eastern time). Economists expect headline CPI to have risen about 0.3% on the month and core CPI, which strips out food and energy, about 0.2%, after gains of 0.6% and 0.3% in September. A smaller boost from gasoline, which fell during October, accounts for most of the expected slowdown in the headline figure. A real-time nowcast from the Cleveland Fed points to readings of about 0.2% for both measures.

The missing piece is a legacy of last year’s 43-day government shutdown, which ran from October 1 to November 12, 2025. The BLS was unable to collect price data that month and never published an October 2025 CPI report. Without a year-ago index, the agency has said it will not publish 12-month changes for October 2026 where the October 2025 data are unavailable, which covers both the all-items and the core series.

That leaves economists to impute last October’s levels and estimate annual inflation themselves. FactSet’s median estimates point to headline inflation of about 4% year on year, up from 3.7% in September, and core inflation of about 2.8%, up from 2.6%. Those figures rest on a small number of forecasts and on imputation choices that vary between firms. Any annual rate quoted after the release will be an estimate rather than an official reading.

Analysts see the risks to core as tilted higher. Elevated shipping costs and reinstated tariffs could lift core goods prices, while airfares, lodging and recreation services may add pressure. A pullback in owners’ equivalent rent after unusual strength in September could offset some of that. Several forecasters note that monthly core readings below 0.15% have been rare since 2022.

The release is the final CPI report before the Federal Reserve’s December meeting. The Fed held rates in October, and an in-line reading would leave inflation well above the 2% target without ruling out further tightening. With no official annual figures, the monthly core number is likely to drive the market reaction.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BlackRock: an AI spending slowdown in 2027 would hurt markets but could also lower yields
item.description:
BlackRock’s two-sided framing helps explain why Treasuries can act as a hedge against AI risk. A slowdown in AI spending would hurt equities but ease the competition for capital that has kept yields elevated. The shift in focus from suppliers to adopters suggests leadership could rotate away from chipmakers and infrastructure names over time, toward companies that show measurable productivity gains. The firm’s question about whether traditional hedges still work, and its call for flexibility, argue against heavy directional bets until AI adoption data firms up. Its 2027 Global Outlook next month is the next marker for positioning.

---

Earlier:

  • Goldman sees $1.5 trillion in AI debt over three years, warns supply weighs on credit
  • WSJ: Anthropic targets Nasdaq debut next week under ticker ANT despite tech selloff

---

BlackRock says the easy part of the AI trade, betting the build-out would happen, is over, and the harder question now is whether adoption can pay for it.

Summary:

  • BlackRock says the AI story is moving into a more nuanced phase, from pricing the build-out to assessing demand, adoption and who benefits
  • A material AI spending slowdown in 2027, while far from certain, could hurt markets, but could also ease competition for capital and lower bond yields
  • That two-sided uncertainty underpinned its move to neutral on US equities and its upgrade of US Treasuries last month
  • AI’s financing needs are colliding with government borrowing and spending on energy security and defence, raising crowding-out questions
  • The higher-rate regime BlackRock has described for five years is now largely priced in, making the outlook less directional
  • The firm’s 2027 Global Outlook is due next month

BlackRock says the AI investment story is entering a more nuanced phase. Attention is moving from the infrastructure build-out to demand, adoption and who ultimately benefits, as competition for capital intensifies.

In its weekly commentary following its 2027 Outlook Forum, the asset manager said last week’s market swings around the US midterm elections illustrated the shift. US stocks rallied the day after Democrats took control of Congress, sold off sharply on Thursday and steadied on Friday. In the first phase of the AI transformation, BlackRock said, the opportunity lay in pricing the conviction that the build-out had to happen. Now investors are weighing the size and speed of that build-out against how quickly AI is adopted and spreads across different tasks.

BlackRock described the risks as two-sided. A material slowdown in AI spending in 2027, which it called far from certain, could have significant adverse consequences for markets. But it could also ease competition for capital and lower bond yields, and its economic fallout could temper some policy initiatives. That uncertainty underpinned the firm’s move to neutral on US equities and its upgrade of US Treasuries last month.

Forum participants debated how much AI capacity will ultimately be built, whether adoption can justify the scale of investment, and when opportunities might shift from suppliers to the companies adopting the technology. They also considered what would happen if spending slowed before productivity gains came through. Another question was who captures the gains and who is disrupted: technology providers, the businesses adopting AI, or their customers.

Competition for capital was a major theme. AI’s extraordinary financing needs are colliding with government borrowing and spending on energy security and defence, which raises the question of whether other borrowers could be crowded out. With credit markets becoming more selective, participants discussed whether more equity issuance could help hyperscalers manage leverage and preserve their borrowing capacity.

More broadly, BlackRock said the supply-driven regime of structurally higher interest rates it has described for five years is now largely priced in, after four years of an AI-driven bull market. That leaves the outlook less directional. Discussions covered shifting global capital flows, changing relationships between stocks, bonds and currencies, opportunities in Europe, China and emerging markets, and the reliability of traditional portfolio hedges. The firm will set out its views in its 2027 Global Outlook next month.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morgan Stanley flags AI as a new risk for the Australian dollar after Democratic sweep
item.description:
Morgan Stanley’s view makes the Australian dollar a cleaner way to trade AI sentiment in FX, which could leave it reacting more to Nasdaq swings than to domestic data in the near term. Today’s China trade data matters as a separate driver, since strong export demand linked to AI hardware could offer some support. Defensive currencies such as the yen and Swiss franc stand to benefit if AI volatility returns. The euro’s inclusion among the bank’s preferred currencies points to a broader rotation away from the US dollar rather than a pure flight to safety. Any concrete state-level action on data centres, particularly in Texas, is the main trigger to watch.

---

AI has become a currency story, and Morgan Stanley’s message is that when AI stocks wobble, the Australian dollar wobbles first.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley says the Australian dollar may lag after the Democratic midterm sweep because it tends to move with sentiment toward AI-driven stocks
  • The bank expects currencies to reflect AI investment uncertainty, more congressional pushback against renewed geopolitical conflict, and a higher risk of targeted trade measures
  • It favours the yen, Swiss franc and euro against the US dollar
  • Morgan Stanley stays overweight global equities and sees the AI capex cycle intact, but flags near-term friction from state-level data centre restrictions, especially in Texas
  • AUD fell about 2.3% last week to around 0.687, its weakest since March and the worst G10 performer

Morgan Stanley has flagged the Australian dollar as vulnerable after the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections. The bank argues that the currency now trades closely with investor sentiment toward AI-driven stocks and is exposed to any regulatory pushback against the AI infrastructure build-out.

In its research on the election results, the bank kept its overweight call on global equities, citing resilient growth, corporate earnings and continued AI investment. It sees the multi-year AI capital spending cycle as intact. But it warned that the results could add near-term friction for AI infrastructure, as newly elected state officials weigh restrictions on data centre development. The bank sees the Texas governor’s race as especially significant. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on a pause in new data centre approvals, in a state that hosts a large share of planned US capacity.

That is where the currency link comes in. Morgan Stanley expects currency markets to reflect uncertainty over AI investment, more pushback in Congress against renewed geopolitical conflict, and a higher risk of targeted trade measures. It favours the Japanese yen, Swiss franc and euro against the US dollar, while the Australian dollar may lag.

The logic rests on the Aussie’s role as a high-beta, pro-cyclical currency. AI has become a central driver of global risk appetite, so a pullback in AI and tech valuations tends to hit growth-sensitive currencies such as the Australian dollar quickly and disproportionately, while defensive currencies attract inflows.

Last week’s price action fits that pattern. The Australian dollar rose at first on election night as the US dollar slipped, but turned sharply lower once the AI selloff took hold. It fell about 2.3% over the week to around 0.687 against the US dollar, its weakest since March, and was the worst performer in the G10. A dovish tone from the Reserve Bank of Australia and a sharp drop in oil prices added to the pressure.

The near-term path is likely to track AI sentiment as much as domestic data. Monday’s rebound in US tech offers some relief. Even so, Morgan Stanley’s view suggests that any renewed wobble in AI stocks, or concrete moves to restrict data centres, would leave the Australian dollar among the first currencies to feel it. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman sees $1.5 trillion in AI debt over three years, warns supply weighs on credit
item.description:
For credit, Goldman’s warning points to more pressure on spreads for AI-exposed investment grade names while the issuance pipeline stays this heavy. New deals may need to come with a concession to attract buyers. The equity raises from Oracle and Meta suggest some of the funding burden is moving onto shareholders, a potential source of dilution worries for stocks already hit by last week’s selloff. For equity investors, the shift in focus from demand to returns argues for more dispersion within the AI complex, rewarding companies that can show margin and free cash flow gains. Together with the wealth managers’ calls to diversify, it adds to the case for broader market leadership.

-

Earlier:

  • WSJ: Anthropic targets Nasdaq debut next week under ticker ANT despite tech selloff

-

The AI build-out is turning into a financing story, and Goldman’s message is that balance sheets and returns, not demand, will decide who comes out ahead.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says more than $110 billion of AI-related bond supply has been announced since October 29, including deals of about $25 billion from Microsoft and $10 billion from Oracle
  • The bank expects AI-related investment grade financing to total around $1.5 trillion over the next three years across bonds, data centre shell financings and chip-backed deals
  • Secondary spreads on the Microsoft deal widened five to ten basis points; Goldman cites supply imbalances and concern over the pace of monetization
  • Hyperscalers have combined operating cash flow of nearly $740 billion and are protecting ratings with equity, including Oracle’s $10 billion issue and Meta’s planned $95 billion raise
  • Upside earnings surprises are fading; investors now focus on converting demand into margins, free cash flow and returns
  • Goldman remains selective on AI credit and expects capital discipline and return on invested capital to determine the next winners

Goldman Sachs expects AI-related investment grade financing to reach around $1.5 trillion over the next three years. The bank warns that the sheer volume of debt coming to market is becoming a strong technical headwind for credit, even as hyperscaler fundamentals remain solid.

In a note on AI from a public investing perspective, Goldman said more than $110 billion of AI-related bond supply has been announced across multiple currencies since October 29. That includes deals of about $25 billion from Microsoft and $10 billion from Oracle. The bank expects future financing to span a range of instruments, from unsecured hyperscaler bonds to data centre shell financings and chip-backed transactions.

Markets are absorbing the supply, but at a price. Goldman pointed to secondary spreads on the Microsoft deal widening by five to ten basis points after the announcement. It attributed moves like that to supply and demand imbalances, as well as some concern about how quickly AI spending will translate into revenue.

The bank was more reassuring on balance sheets. It said the hyperscalers retain a large cash buffer, with combined operating cash flow of nearly $740 billion, and appear committed to protecting their credit ratings by diversifying how they fund themselves. Goldman cited Oracle’s $10 billion equity issue alongside its bond deal, and Meta’s planned $95 billion equity raise, as signs that companies are managing the ratings impact of their capital plans. Even so, it said it remains selective on credit in the sector.

On equities, Goldman said this earnings season has brought diminishing upside surprises as AI spending settles into a steady, multi-year ramp. Strong demand alone is becoming less of a differentiator. Investors increasingly want to know whether that demand can be met and how efficiently it turns into margins, free cash flow and shareholder returns.

Monetization is uneven, according to the bank. Newer consumer AI formats currently earn less than traditional search. Even so, Goldman noted that Google’s AI Overviews has reached 1 billion users and monetizes at core search rates, and that a quarter of users of Meta’s Muse agent use it to make purchases. Enterprise adoption is steady rather than accelerating sharply. Demand for custom AI infrastructure is strong, while uptake of off-the-shelf tools is more gradual.

Goldman’s conclusion is that AI is becoming a test of capital and operational discipline as much as of technology. It expects the next generation of winners to be decided by balance-sheet capacity, pricing discipline and return on invested capital. That favours companies that can turn large order books into clean margin expansion.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Iran tells US to stop ‘fake news’ on talks, demands it accept seven conditions to end war
item.description:
For oil, Rezaei’s remarks undercut the de-escalation reading of Trump’s post. Washington’s preferred status quo is the blockade staying in place, while Tehran wants it lifted first, so there is no visible route to restoring normal Hormuz flows. A lower risk of renewed strikes may trim the war premium at the margin, but the supply squeeze looks set to persist. Crude dips on peace headlines may stay shallow. Iran’s history of dismissing reported talks also suggests traders should discount optimistic diplomatic headlines until both sides confirm them.

---

Trump sees momentum toward peace while Tehran sees no talks at all, and the blockade both sides keep invoking is what stands between them.

Summary:

  • Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei told the US to stop publishing false reports about what he called imaginary negotiations
  • He said it was time for Washington to accept the seven conditions Iran has repeatedly set out, and that the war had done serious damage to the US government
  • Iran conveyed the conditions through Qatar in September; the three named publicly are an end to the war on all fronts, release of frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade
  • Tehran says it will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz to normal traffic until the conditions are met
  • The remarks contrast with Trump’s view of “positive momentum” and his comment that Gulf states prefer to keep the blockade in place

Iran’s top security official told Washington to stop publishing “fake news” about what he called imaginary negotiations. He said the time had come for the United States to accept the seven conditions Tehran has repeatedly set out for ending the war.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, also said the conflict had done serious damage to the US government. His remarks on Monday contrast sharply with US President Donald Trump’s message. After a call with Qatar’s prime minister, Trump said he sees positive momentum toward ending the conflict and that renewed US military action looks unlikely. He also said Gulf states would prefer to keep the current US naval blockade of Iran in place, alongside a new effort to choke off Iran’s land routes.

Tehran first conveyed its seven conditions to Washington through Qatari mediators in September. Rezaei has not published the full list, but he has named three central demands: an end to the war on all fronts, the release of frozen Iranian funds and an end to the US naval blockade. Iran has also said it will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz to normal traffic until those conditions are met, and that this point is not up for negotiation.

Denials of talks have become a recurring feature of the conflict. Iranian officials have repeatedly rejected US and media reports of negotiations, at times accusing Washington of using such reports to move oil and financial markets. Iran has, however, acknowledged that messages continue to pass through mediators including Qatar and Pakistan.

For oil, the comments are a reminder that the two sides remain far apart. Trump’s description of a status quo built on the blockade runs directly against Iran’s demand that the blockade be lifted first. That leaves little sign of a near-term path to restoring normal flows through Hormuz, even if the risk of renewed large-scale strikes has eased. Any rally in risk appetite built on de-escalation hopes could prove fragile while the standoff lasts. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Asset managers stay constructive on stocks after AI rout, urge investors to diversify
item.description:
The managers’ readiness to buy the dip helps explain why Monday’s rebound came so quickly. It also suggests dips in AI names will keep drawing buyers unless state-level curbs on data centres turn out to be more than marginal. Falling bond yields during the selloff point to easier financial conditions, which supports equities overall rather than just the crowded mega-cap trade. The call to diversify implies money moving toward small caps, emerging markets, infrastructure and shorter-duration credit, so leadership could broaden even if headline tech indices recover. Texas data centre policy is the main risk to that view.

---

Earlier:

  • WSJ: Anthropic targets Nasdaq debut next week under ticker ANT despite tech selloff

---

Wealth managers see last week’s AI rout as a shakeout of crowded positions, not the end of the AI cycle, and their advice is to spread the bets.

Summary:

  • Wealth managers broadly remain constructive on equities after Thursday’s selloff, seeing a reset in crowded AI positioning rather than a lasting downturn
  • The S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Nasdaq 5.5% on Thursday, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down about 12% and around 38% below its June level
  • Some managers see the federal political risk as overstated, with state curbs such as those in Texas the more tangible threat to data centre growth
  • Falling bond yields were read as a sign of contained inflation and slower but sustainable growth, not recession
  • Diversification is the common advice: small caps, emerging markets, infrastructure, asset-backed securities and shorter-duration credit
  • The views were gathered before Monday’s rebound in US stocks

Wealth managers are largely sticking with a constructive view on equities after last Thursday’s sharp selloff in US technology stocks. They argue that the slide reflected a reset in crowded positioning rather than a break in the AI investment cycle. Their common message is that investors should diversify rather than retreat. The views were gathered before Monday’s rebound in US stocks.

The selloff was triggered by concerns that Democratic gains in the US midterm elections could bring tighter regulation of AI and new limits on data centre construction, slowing the infrastructure build-out. It reversed an initial post-election rally. The S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Nasdaq 5.5% on Thursday. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped about 12%, taking its decline since June to around 38%. The pressure carried into Friday, with tech-heavy North Asian markets leading losses.

Several managers see the political risk as overstated. One noted that AI still has bipartisan support as a strategic priority and that any federal restrictions would face a presidential veto. In that view, the more concrete threat comes from states such as Texas curbing new data centre projects. That would slow development at the margin without halting it.

Others pointed to signals from bond markets. Yields have kept falling through the equity selloff. One manager read that as evidence that inflation fears remain contained and that the bond market is pricing slower but sustainable growth, not recession. That firm described corrections of this size as opportunities to add exposure and said it had already rebalanced.

Diversification was the dominant theme. Advisers highlighted global small caps, emerging markets, infrastructure, asset-backed securities and shorter-duration credit as areas that either held up better or offer different return drivers. One investment chief said his firm had been moving underweight US mega-cap technology through the year in favour of an equal-weighted index. He argued there is no tech bubble to burst, just a broadening of returns to other stocks.

In Asia, analysts expect near-term volatility as markets weigh possible delays to US data centre construction. Over time, they argue, compute capacity can shift abroad, potentially benefiting Asian supply chains, while China builds out its own AI ecosystem. Some see the selling as having pushed quality stocks below what their fundamentals justify, creating value for active investors.

One manager added some perspective: this is roughly the fifth sharp fall in AI-linked stocks in the past 12 months, and the sector has recovered each time. Monday’s bounce will be an early test of whether that pattern holds.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump says renewed Iran strikes ‘quite unlikely’ as Gulf allies back blockade status quo
item.description:
For oil, the post cuts both ways. A lower risk of renewed US strikes should erode some of the war premium that pushed Brent above $120 in April. But the status quo the Gulf states reportedly favour keeps Iranian crude off the market. Tehran has also tied reopening the Strait of Hormuz to the blockade being lifted. That leaves prices with a supply-driven floor even as the escalation risk fades. Without a deal that restores normal Hormuz traffic, dips on de-escalation headlines may struggle to run far.

-

Trump is talking down the risk of renewed strikes on Iran but not the pressure, with Gulf allies said to favour a blockade by land and sea over a return to war.

Summary:

  • Trump said renewed US military action against Iran seems “quite unlikely” after a call with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani
  • He said Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and others prefer the status quo: the US naval blockade plus the new Iron Gate land effort
  • All sides agree Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, which Trump called non-negotiable; he said the US stays ready to act if conditions change
  • US Central Command set up Task Force Iron Gate on Saturday to disrupt Iranian weapons and sanctioned-goods transit by land and across the Caspian Sea
  • CENTCOM says the sea blockade has prevented more than $25 billion of Iranian crude exports in recent months
  • Trump cited “positive momentum” toward ending the conflict

US President Donald Trump said renewed military action against Iran now looks “quite unlikely,” after a call with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani. The signal is that Washington will keep squeezing Tehran through blockades rather than fresh strikes.

In a post on his Truth Social platform on Monday, Trump said Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait and other regional states would prefer to keep the status quo. He defined that as continuing the US naval blockade of Iranian ports alongside the newly launched Iron Gate effort, which together cover Iran by land and sea. Trump said all parties agree Iran cannot be allowed a nuclear weapon and called that non-negotiable. He added that the US remains ready to act if conditions in the region change, but said he sees positive momentum toward ending the conflict.

US Central Command announced the Iron Gate initiative on Saturday. It is a task force of about 20 civilian and military staff based in Tampa, Florida. Its job is to disrupt Iranian movement of weapons, dual-use technology and sanctioned goods across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea. CENTCOM said the sea blockade, which covers Iranian ports on the Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, has stopped Iran exporting more than $25 billion of crude in recent months.

The message points two ways for oil. A lower risk of a return to large-scale strikes, which helped drive Brent above $120 in April, chips away at the war premium. But the status quo the Gulf states reportedly favour keeps Iranian barrels off the market. Tehran has also made lifting the blockade a condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz to normal traffic. Brent rebounded to around $98 on Friday from a two-month low, as tanker attacks in the Gulf offset expectations of de-escalation after the US midterm elections.

For traders, the post points to a long holding pattern rather than a resolution. Without a deal that reopens Hormuz, supply concerns are likely to keep a floor under prices even as the threat of renewed escalation fades. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: WSJ: Anthropic targets Nasdaq debut next week under ticker ANT despite tech selloff
item.description:
Anthropic’s listing has become a test of how much appetite for AI risk survived last week’s rout. A range that holds near $1.5 trillion would suggest institutional demand is intact and could help steady AI-linked names on the Nasdaq. A sharply lower range, or a delay, would look like confirmation that sector valuations are resetting. A deal this size could also pull money from the same funds that hold megacap tech, a possible near-term drag as they make room. The filing due this week, with the range, the share count and any anchor investors, is the next catalyst.

---

Bounce on Monday for stocks:

  • investingLive Americas market news wrap: Iran optimism and tech rebound leads to risk surge

---

Anthropic is betting last week’s AI selloff was a wobble, not a verdict, and is pressing on with its IPO while investors talk the price down.

Summary:

  • Anthropic plans to go ahead with its IPO later this month, aiming for shares to start trading next Thursday or Friday, the WSJ reported
  • A filing due early this week is expected to set out the valuation range, the number of shares and the price, and may name anchor investors
  • Investors had expected a target near $1.5 trillion, but some are now pushing lower after Thursday’s AI rout, well below the $2 trillion floated months ago
  • Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are advising on the range; the shares will list on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT”
  • The Nasdaq Composite lost about $2.5 trillion in value on Thursday after the midterm elections boosted AI sceptics and data centre moratoriums
  • Rival OpenAI recently raised less than half its target at about $1.25 trillion; SpaceX’s record June IPO raised around $75 billion

Anthropic plans to press ahead with its initial public offering later this month despite a sharp selloff in artificial intelligence stocks, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The maker of the Claude AI models has meetings lined up with key investors this week and is aiming for its shares to begin trading on the Nasdaq next Thursday or Friday under the ticker “ANT.”

The valuation is now the central question. Anthropic is expected to set out its target range in a filing early this week. The filing will also show how many shares it plans to sell and at what price, and could reveal that some large investors have already agreed to buy at the IPO price. A week ago, investors expected the company to aim for around $1.5 trillion. Since last Thursday’s slide in AI stocks, some major investors have been pushing for less, according to the Journal. Anthropic will almost certainly have to accept a figure well below the roughly $2 trillion floated months ago.

Company executives have been working with bankers from Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley on where to set the range. The trade-off is a familiar one. Aim too high and demand could suffer, with shares falling after the debut. Aim too low and the company and its advisers risk criticism for leaving money on the table. Banks sometimes favour a slightly lower-than-expected opening range that can later be raised on strong demand.

The backdrop has turned against AI names. Companies in the Nasdaq Composite lost about $2.5 trillion in value on Thursday after the US midterm elections swept a bloc of AI sceptics into office and passed moratoriums that could slow data centre construction. The index has since recovered some ground, which is likely to have encouraged Anthropic to proceed. Even before the vote, enthusiasm for AI stocks had been fading on worries over the scale of spending and uncertain returns. Rival OpenAI raised less than half its initial target in its latest funding round, at a lower-than-hoped valuation of around $1.25 trillion.

Anthropic could still choose to wait for calmer conditions, though the Journal noted that a delay would risk sparking panic in the market. The yardstick is SpaceX, whose record June offering raised around $75 billion at a valuation of nearly $1.8 trillion. This week’s filing should show how close Anthropic can get. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Event calendar in Asia Tuesday, November 10, 2026: BoJ and China trade data
item.description:
BoJ Summary of Opinions and China trade data: what to watch in Asia on Tuesday

Bank of Japan: Summary of Opinions (October 29-30 meeting)

The Bank of Japan releases the Summary of Opinions from its October 29 and 30 policy meeting at 23:50 GMT on Monday (18:50 US Eastern time).

The Summary is a short, anonymous digest of the views board members and government representatives gave at the meeting. It comes out about a week and a half after the decision. Speakers are not named, and the governor, as chair, edits the document. Its value is speed: it gives an early read on where the debate stands, how many members lean toward the next move, and what conditions they want met first. The minutes are a different product. They come out only after the following meeting, so the October minutes are due on December 23, after the December decision. They give a fuller account of the discussion, but by then they are largely history. The Summary is the one that can move the yen.

At the meeting the BoJ held its policy rate at 1.25%, a 31-year high, on an 8-1 vote. Board member Hajime Takata dissented and proposed a hike to 1.5%, on the view that underlying inflation has reached the 2% target. The Bank said underlying inflation is now generally consistent with its target and that risks to prices are skewed to the upside. It raised its fiscal 2027 core inflation forecast to 2.6% from 2.4% and trimmed growth to 0.7%. It also surprised markets by more than doubling the pace of its ETF sales to around 860 billion yen a year from January 2027. Governor Kazuo Ueda then softened the inflation message at his press conference.

The focus is December. The BoJ raised rates in June and September, and markets widely expect it to keep that quarterly pace with a hike to 1.5% at the December 17-18 meeting. Watch how many members say conditions for the next step are in place, whether anyone else shares Takata’s sense of urgency, and whether the more cautious members point to the softer growth outlook or to oil-driven import costs. A Summary heavy with near-term hike support would firm December pricing and help the yen. A guarded tone would leave the timing open.

China: October trade data

China publishes October trade figures on Tuesday. A Reuters poll expects exports to have grown about 33% year on year in dollar terms, slightly slower than September’s 36% surge, with imports seen up around 32%. The surplus is expected near $126 billion, down from about $134 billion in September but enough to take the total for the first ten months of 2026 above $1 trillion. Demand for AI infrastructure hardware has driven the export boom, though some analysts read October’s fall in new export orders as an early warning that the tech cycle is softening.

The equity backdrop matters more. The CSI 300 fell 8.5% in October, its worst month in over a decade, and posted a record 12 straight weekly losses on a weak economy and doubts about AI earnings. Beijing first called on state funds, the so-called “national team,” to buy shares and on companies to step up buybacks. On November 2 the PBOC and the securities regulator brought back the 2024 toolkit. They are expanding the swap facility that funds stock purchases by brokers, funds and insurers. They cut the relending rate for buybacks to 1% from 1.25% and made that facility permanent. They also eased the rules on buybacks. Investors were sceptical at first, and the state funds then bought more. So the Bank of Japan is speeding up its ETF sales while Beijing’s state funds are buying. A strong trade print may help sentiment at the margin, but analysts argue a lasting turnaround needs household-focused fiscal support and a steadier property market. 

Bank of Japan Governor Ueda 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Anthropic unveils Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 models ahead of IPO
item.description:
If you're about to ask investors for $100 billion, it's a good time to have something new to sell.

Anthropic today launched Claude Fable 5.2 and its unrestricted counterpart, Mythos 5.2, with the company claiming another significant leap in performance at a lower price. The first impression isn't great, as it doesn't look like a big leap forward.

The timing is notable as Anthropic prepares for what could be the largest IPO in history, potentially raising $80 billion to $100 billion at a valuation of as much as $1.75 trillion.

The company says the new models outperform Opus 5.5 on nearly every benchmark it tested, including a win over OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra in agentic coding. Fable 5.2 scored 69.9% on FrontierSWE v2 compared to 65.5% for Astra.

From the PR:

Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

That's about 20% cheaper than the prior benchmarks.

For investors, the price cut might be the most important part of the announcement.

One of the biggest questions surrounding the AI trade is whether the economics ultimately work. There's little doubt about demand but the costs of delivering increasingly powerful models remain enormous.

Anthropic says Fable 5.2 running at High effort can match Opus 5.5 at Max effort on coding tasks at roughly half the cost.

That's a meaningful improvement and it fits with what we've seen throughout the AI boom but it's not some kind of revolution that will get the market frothing for hte IPO.

Anthropic also says Claude now writes more than 90% of the code merged into its own core codebase. That's the kind of statistic that will feature prominently in an IPO roadshow.

There are also signs that the economics are improving. Compute costs have fallen from 172% of revenue to 57% over the past year. That remains an expensive business, but it's a dramatic improvement and one that suggests there's more to come.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: NZDUSD buyers are starting to take back control after reaching the lowest level since April 2025
item.description:
The dollar gives back gains. The kiwi gets an extra lift.

The NZDUSD fell to its lowest level since April 2025 on Friday, reaching 0.5527 before closing the week at 0.55426. The pair is higher today as the US dollar gives back some of Friday’s gains and New Zealand’s election gives the kiwi an extra lift.

On the US side, hopes for progress in diplomacy with Iran helped push crude oil lower and eased haven demand for the dollar. That reversed part of Friday’s USD rally, which followed the strong US jobs report.

On the New Zealand side, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s National-led coalition holds 67 of 131 seats in the preliminary count, one seat above the majority threshold. That gives the incumbents a path to stay in power and reduces the near-term odds that an employment objective will be restored alongside the RBNZ’s inflation objective. Markets could read such a change as dovish. About 400,000 special votes are still outstanding, with final results due November 27.

Buyers reclaim the old floor and defend the 100-hour moving average.

On the hourly chart, the first step was a move back above the old floor near 0.55791. That opened the door to the 100-hour moving average at 0.5599. Buyers pushed through that level and tested the 200-hour moving average at 0.56114 before the price rotated lower.

The important part was what happened on the pullback. Buyers leaned against the 100-hour moving average and pushed the price back up to its highest level since Thursday. That puts the next swing area at 0.5625 to 0.5633 in focus.

What next for traders?

A move through 0.5633 would have traders looking toward last week’s high near 0.5657. Above that, the 38.2% retracement of the move down from the August high comes in at 0.57026.

The trading rule is simple. As long as the price holds above the 100-hour moving average at 0.5599, the buyers can stay in the game and work through those targets one at a time. A move back below that average would weaken the rebound and put the old floor near 0.55791 back in play.

In the video above, I walk through the rebound on the hourly chart, show why 0.5599 is the barometer for buyers, and lay out the levels they need to clear to extend the move.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Barkin: Jobs report was 'healthy' but firms still see low-hire, low-fire economy
item.description:
Comments from Barkin:

  • No base case for Dec meeting
  • Hard to know impact of elections on economy
  • Current policy rate likely around or slightly below neutral
  • Do not think ballot measures will impede data center construction, companies will find somewhere else to build

'Slightly below' neutral is a new talking point and it's a surprise given that Fed funds are almost at 4%. For him, it would signal that rates could go up more than the 50 bps priced into the market in the next year.

item.title: U.S. Treasury sells $58 billion of 3 year notes at a high yield of 4.627%
item.description:
• WI level at the time of the auction: 4.622%

  • High yield: 4.627%

  • Tail: 0.5 basis points vs an average stop-through of 0.1 basis point

  • Bid to cover: 2.53X vs the average of 2.64X

  • Directs: 35.0% vs the average of 25.2%

  • Indirects: 55.5% vs the average of 62.7%

  • Dealers: 9.5% vs the average of 12.1%

Auction grade: C−

The auction was a little below average. The high yield came in 0.5 basis points above the when-issued level, and the bid to cover fell short of its average. Indirect bidders took a smaller share than usual, but direct bidders stepped up, taking 35.0% against an average of 25.2%. That helped keep the dealer takedown below average at 9.5%. The strong direct demand softened the result, but the tail and lighter overall bidding tipped the grade to a C−.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: USDCAD trades back near unchanged as buyers return
item.description:
Recall that USDCAD moved sharply higher on Friday after a stronger US jobs report and a weaker Canadian jobs report. The contrast favored the US dollar, and the price action followed. Buyers took the pair above its 100-period moving average on the 4-hour chart, currently at 1.40289, and its 100-day moving average at 1.40423.

The momentum carried the price through the 1.4068–1.4081 swing area, above the 200-period moving average on the 4-hour chart at 1.41209, and past 1.41297, the low of the next swing area. The move ultimately reached 1.4139.

Sellers had their shot. Buyers stepped back in.

Broad US dollar selling early today gave back some of Friday’s gains. USDCAD slipped below the 38.2% retracement of the move up from the August low at 1.40828 and reached 1.4078, inside the 1.4068–1.4081 swing area. That is where buyers stepped back in. The rebound has taken the price back above the 200-period moving average and up to Friday’s high near 1.4139.

What next for buyers?

A break above 1.4139 would have traders looking toward 1.41532, the high of the swing area that starts at 1.41297. Get and stay above 1.41532, and the next upside target is the 1.4192–1.4204 swing area.

On the downside, the 200-period moving average at 1.41209 is the close risk level. If the price gets back below it and starts to trade comfortably there, it would take some of the steam out of the rebound. Traders would then look back toward the 38.2% retracement at 1.40828 and the swing area just below it.

The trading lesson

Friday’s high tells traders whether buyers can extend the move. The moving average tells them where the rebound starts to lose traction. Keeping those two levels separate gives buyers a nearby level to lean against while they wait to see if the next break can hold.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.
